title: Understanding PCOS
subtitle: What every woman should know about Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

sections.heading: What is PCOS?
sections.body: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is one of the most common hormonal disorders affecting women of reproductive age. It occurs when the ovaries produce excess androgens (male hormones), leading to a range of symptoms that can affect your menstrual cycle, fertility, appearance, and overall health.

sections.heading: Common Signs and Symptoms
sections.body:
PCOS can show up differently in every woman, but the most common signs include:

- Irregular or absent periods
- Excess hair growth on the face, chest, or back (hirsutism)
- Acne and oily skin
- Weight gain, especially around the belly
- Difficulty getting pregnant (infertility)
- Dark patches of skin (acanthosis nigricans)
- Thinning hair on the scalp

sections.heading: What Causes PCOS?
sections.body:
The exact cause of PCOS is not fully understood, but it is believed to be a combination of factors:

- Genetics: PCOS tends to run in families
- Insulin resistance: Many women with PCOS have cells that don't respond well to insulin, causing the body to produce more insulin, which in turn triggers the ovaries to produce more androgens
- Chronic low-grade inflammation: This can also contribute to androgen production

sections.heading: How is PCOS Diagnosed?
sections.body:
There is no single test for PCOS. Diagnosis is typically based on:

- Your medical history and symptoms
- A physical exam
- Blood tests to check hormone levels and rule out other conditions
- An ultrasound to look at your ovaries

Doctors usually diagnose PCOS using the Rotterdam criteria: you need at least two of three signs (irregular periods, high androgen levels, or polycystic ovaries on ultrasound).

sections.heading: Managing PCOS
sections.body:
While there is no cure for PCOS, it can be effectively managed:

- Lifestyle changes: Regular exercise and a balanced diet can help manage weight and improve insulin sensitivity
- Medications: Birth control pills can regulate periods and reduce androgen levels. Metformin may help with insulin resistance
- Fertility treatments: If you are trying to conceive, medications like letrozole or clomiphene can help stimulate ovulation
- Hair and skin treatments: Addressing acne, excess hair, and skin darkening with appropriate treatments

Remember, PCOS is manageable, and with the right approach, you can lead a healthy and fulfilling life. Always consult your healthcare provider for personalized advice.

title: Hormones 101
subtitle: Understanding the chemical messengers that run your body

sections.heading: What Are Hormones?
sections.body: Hormones are chemical messengers produced by glands in your endocrine system. They travel through your bloodstream and tell your organs what to do. In women, hormones play a crucial role in regulating the menstrual cycle, metabolism, mood, sleep, and reproductive health.

sections.heading: Key Female Hormones
sections.body:
Estrogen: The primary female sex hormone. It regulates the menstrual cycle, supports bone health, and influences mood and skin.

Progesterone: Prepares the uterus for pregnancy and helps maintain early pregnancy. It rises after ovulation and falls before your period.

Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH): Stimulates the growth of eggs in the ovaries.

Luteinizing Hormone (LH): Triggers ovulation — the release of an egg from the ovary.

Testosterone: Present in small amounts in women, it affects libido, energy, and muscle mass.

Cortisol: The stress hormone. Chronic high cortisol can disrupt your menstrual cycle and affect sleep.

sections.heading: Hormones and Your Cycle
sections.body:
Your menstrual cycle is a beautiful orchestration of hormones:

Days 1-5 (Menstruation): Estrogen and progesterone are at their lowest, causing the uterine lining to shed.

Days 6-13 (Follicular Phase): FSH rises, stimulating egg development. Estrogen builds up the uterine lining.

Day 14 (Ovulation): A surge in LH triggers the release of a mature egg.

Days 15-28 (Luteal Phase): Progesterone rises to maintain the uterine lining. If no pregnancy occurs, both hormones drop, and the cycle restarts.

sections.heading: Signs of Hormonal Imbalance
sections.body:
Hormonal imbalances can manifest as:

- Irregular or painful periods
- Severe PMS symptoms
- Unexplained weight gain or difficulty losing weight
- Acne, especially along the jawline
- Hair thinning or excess facial hair
- Fatigue and low energy
- Mood swings, anxiety, or depression
- Difficulty sleeping

If you experience persistent symptoms, consult a healthcare provider who can run hormone level tests and recommend appropriate treatment.

title: Iron-Rich Foods
subtitle: Essential nutrition for healthy periods and energy

sections.heading: Why Iron Matters
sections.body: Iron is essential for producing hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout your body. During menstruation, you lose blood and with it, iron. Many women in India are at risk of iron deficiency, which can lead to fatigue, weakness, dizziness, and difficulty concentrating.

sections.heading: How Much Iron Do You Need?
sections.body:
Women of reproductive age need about 18 mg of iron per day. This increases to 27 mg during pregnancy. Post-menopausal women need about 8 mg per day.

Women with heavy periods may need even more iron to compensate for greater blood loss.

sections.heading: Best Iron-Rich Foods
sections.body:
Heme iron (from animal sources, absorbed better):
- Red meat and liver
- Chicken and turkey
- Fish (tuna, sardines, salmon)
- Eggs

Non-heme iron (from plant sources):
- Spinach and other dark leafy greens
- Lentils (masoor dal) and chickpeas
- Kidney beans (rajma) and black beans
- Tofu and soy products
- Jaggery (gur) — a traditional Indian sweetener rich in iron
- Dates and raisins
- Pumpkin seeds and sesame seeds
- Fortified cereals

sections.heading: Tips to Boost Iron Absorption
sections.body:
Pair iron-rich foods with vitamin C sources (citrus fruits, tomatoes, bell peppers) to increase absorption by up to 6 times.

Avoid drinking tea or coffee with iron-rich meals — the tannins can block absorption.

Cook in a cast-iron skillet, which can increase the iron content of your food.

If you are vegetarian or vegan, pay extra attention to combining plant-based iron sources with vitamin C-rich foods.
